beats.narration: Begin by framing Defining the Problem Space as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Consider this worked case: Given a list of integers, output the sum of all positive values. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Defining the Problem Space
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a text box containing the problem statement and two sample input/output pairs side by side.

beats.narration: Now define Core Data Structures precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Consider this worked case: A queue is appropriate for processing tasks in the order they arrive, while a stack models undo operations. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Core Data Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a diagram with five labeled boxes (List, Stack, Queue, Tree, Graph) each containing a simple icon representing its structure.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Decomposition and Abstraction operates in a concrete sequence. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Consider this worked case: Create a function `sum_positive` that takes a list and returns an integer, isolating the logic from the main program. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Decomposition and Abstraction
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a flowchart with a top-level box labeled 'Main' branching to a sub-box labeled 'sum_positive' with arrows indicating data flow.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Control Flow and Recursion and make the decision criteria explicit. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Consider this worked case: A recursive factorial function computes n! by calling itself with n-1 until the base case n=0 is reached. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Control Flow and Recursion
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a call stack diagram showing nested frames for factorial(3) expanding to factorial(2), factorial(1), and factorial(0).

beats.narration: Apply State, Identity, and Namespaces to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Consider this worked case: Two variables `a` and `b` can both reference the same list object, so modifying `a` also changes `b`. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: State, Identity, and Namespaces
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a memory map with two name labels pointing to a single box labeled 'list object' and a separate box for a distinct integer.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Exceptions and Error Handling, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. Consider this worked case: Attempting to divide by zero raises a ZeroDivisionError that must be caught to prevent program termination. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Exceptions and Error Handling
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a timeline where normal execution is interrupted by a red 'Exception' marker, followed by a handler block.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Correctness and Testing with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases. Consider this worked case: Test the sorting function with an empty list, a single element, and a list with duplicate values to verify edge cases. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Correctness and Testing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a table with three rows labeled 'Empty', 'Single', 'Duplicates' and columns for 'Input', 'Expected Output', and 'Actual Output'.

beats.narration: Use Algorithm Selection Criteria to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Problem solving skills and the choice and application of appropriate algorithms and data structures are at the core of the course. Consider this worked case: Binary search requires a sorted list; using it on an unsorted list violates the invariant and yields incorrect results. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Algorithm Selection Criteria
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a decision tree: start node 'Is data sorted?' branches to 'Yes → Binary Search' and 'No → Linear Search'.

beats.narration: Connect Design and Implementation Workflow to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Consider this worked case: Before coding, write a contract specifying preconditions (e. g. , non-empty list) and postconditions (e. g. , returned sum equals total of positives). Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Design and Implementation Workflow
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a three-step process diagram: '1. Problem Statement', '2. Design (contracts, data structures)', '3. Implementation'.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns. Consider this worked case: Checklist items: Verify syntax with a linter, run unit tests on edge cases, trace execution with print statements, and review logical invariants. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a checklist graphic with four tick boxes labeled 'Syntax', 'Edge Cases', 'Trace', 'Invariant Review'.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: This course serves as a means of bringing transfer students with some programming and data structures background to the same skill level that the computer science program's first year students have after completing CSCI 141 and 142. Problem solving skills and the choice and application of appropriate algorithms and data structures are at the core of the course. Assignments (both in class and for homework) requiring a design and an implementation are an integral part of the course. Larger programming projects are also required. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 6 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective, GE: Mathematical Perspective, NTID Math Processes, SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

sources.excerpt: The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace.
